sections.html:
The Register of Deeds works from 375 Church Street, Suite 106, Dayton, TN 37321, and the number to call is 423-775-7841.

Land records in Tennessee are kept by the county, so a deed for any Rhea County house goes to this one counter. That holds for Dayton, Graysville, Spring City and the rural parts of the county alike. Phone ahead before you make the drive. Ask for the current recording fee schedule, the hours on the day you plan to visit, and whether staff want the signed original or will take another format.

sections.h2: What does it cost to record a deed in Rhea County?
sections.html:
The register sets a per-page recording fee, and the way to learn the current figure is to call 423-775-7841. The tax portion is fixed by the state and makes up the larger share of the bill on most sales.

Tennessee recordation taxes collected at the register
State recordation chargeRate
Realty transfer tax on a deed$0.37 per $100
Mortgage (indebtedness) tax on a deed of trust$0.115 per $100, first $2,000 exempt

The page fee for the register's own work is added to each total.

sections.h2: Transfer tax on a Rhea County home sale
sections.html:
The realty transfer tax is $0.37 per $100. State Revenue Department guidance says it applies to all transfers of realty and is generally based on the greater of the price paid or the property's value, citing Tenn. Code Ann. 67-4-409.

Since the rule picks the greater of price or value, a deed that states a very low price on a house worth more will not shrink the tax. If you are planning a family sale or one below market, talk to the title agent about the figure before the deed is signed. A buyer's lender adds a second charge when the deed of trust is recorded: the indebtedness tax of $0.115 per $100 of the loan after the first $2,000.

The sale contract decides which side pays each line, so read the settlement statement ahead of closing day. If the total at the counter differs from the title company's estimate, ask the staff to walk through it with you.

sections.h2: Which Rhea County offices handle the rest of a sale?
sections.html:
The deed is only one stop. The other two property offices share the same building at 375 Church Street in Dayton.

  • Rhea County Property Assessor, Suite 100, 423-775-7840: parcel values and ownership maps
  • Rhea County Trustee, Suite 110, 423-775-7810: property tax bills and payoff amounts
  • Rhea County Register of Deeds, Suite 106, 423-775-7841: recording of the deed and mortgage

The order matters at closing. Get a tax payoff from the Trustee, send it to the title company, and have the register record the deed afterward. Ask the Trustee which year's bill is open and whether interest or delinquent amounts are attached, because back taxes are paid from the sale proceeds.

sections.h2: Questions to ask the register before you close
sections.html:
A short list saves a second trip. Put these to the staff at 423-775-7841.

  • What is the total recording fee for a deed of my page count?
  • Does the deed need any reference to a prior book and page?
  • Has the office received the release for the mortgage being paid off?
  • How will the recorded original be returned, and how long does it take?
  • Can a title company record by an electronic method, or does it need to deliver the paper?

Answers apply on the day you ask, and fees and forms can change. If you sell as-is to a buyer who pays cash, the deed is usually the only document at the register, so the visit is quick when the paperwork is ready.

sections.h2: How a Rhea County sale moves from contract to recorded deed
sections.html:
Most of the steps happen before anyone visits the courthouse. Here is the usual order for a seller.

  1. Sign the sale contract, which settles who pays the transfer tax and the recording fees.
  2. Have the title company confirm who holds title. A deed still in a relative's name has to be resolved before a buyer can close.
  3. Collect the tax payoff from the Trustee and the lien release from any lender being paid.
  4. Sign the deed with a notary, then let the title company deliver it for recording.
  5. Keep a copy of the recorded deed with your closing papers.

Sellers who inherited a house should bring the recorded chain of deeds to an attorney or title company before listing, since gaps in the chain are the most common cause of delay.

sections.h2: What to bring when you visit the Dayton office
sections.html:
Call first, then arrive with the paperwork complete so the counter visit is short. A clerk can only record what is in front of them, and an incomplete packet means a second trip across the county.

  • The signed and notarized deed, as an original unless staff say another format works.
  • Payment for the state tax and the register's per-page fee, in whatever form staff tell you they accept.
  • The names of the parties spelled exactly as they appear on the prior deed.
  • The book and page of the previous recording, if your title agent has it.
  • A phone number where the office can reach you if something is missing.

Mismatched name spellings are a quiet source of delay. A deed that calls the seller one thing when the chain of title calls the seller another can send the title company back to fix it. Reading the earlier deed against your own ahead of time takes a few minutes and prevents most of that.

sections.h2: Why recording order matters for a seller
sections.html:
Recording is what puts the sale on the public record. Until the deed is filed, the buyer's ownership is not visible to anyone searching the books, and the Assessor does not know to update the parcel. Delays between signing and recording are normally short, but a seller should still ask the title company when the filing will happen.

A mortgage payoff works the same way in reverse. The lender releases its lien once it is paid, and the release is recorded so the title shows clean. If the release has not reached the register by closing, the title company may hold back part of your proceeds until it does. Asking the staff whether the release has arrived is one of the simplest ways to avoid that.

Rhea County has an estimated 34,844 residents as of July 1, 2025, up 4.8 percent from the April 2020 base. It has 15,955 housing units and 13,475 households, and owners live in 71.5 percent of occupied homes. The median owner-occupied value is $206,000 for 2020 to 2024. Owners with a mortgage report median monthly costs of $1,326, and owners without one report $365. Median gross rent is $839. Dayton is the county seat and largest town, with Graysville and Spring City as the other towns.

faqs.q: Where do I record a deed for a house in Rhea County?
faqs.a: At the Rhea County Register of Deeds, 375 Church Street, Suite 106, Dayton, TN 37321. The phone number is 423-775-7841.

faqs.q: How much is the Tennessee transfer tax on a Rhea County sale?
faqs.a: It is $0.37 per $100, generally on the greater of the price paid or the property's value. The register's own recording fee is added on top.

faqs.q: Is there a mortgage tax in Rhea County?
faqs.a: Yes. Tennessee charges $0.115 per $100 of indebtedness when a deed of trust is recorded, and the first $2,000 is exempt.

faqs.q: Who gets my property tax payoff in Rhea County?
faqs.a: The Rhea County Trustee, 375 Church Street, Suite 110, at 423-775-7810. Ask for the open balance and any interest to your closing date, and give it to the title company.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Rhea County house if the deed is still in a parent's name?
faqs.a: A title agent has to resolve who holds title before a buyer can close. Ask the register at 423-775-7841 what the recorded chain of deeds shows, and bring the findings to an attorney or title company.
